 Michelle R. Fajman, director of the Lake County Board of Elections and Registration, describes the number of voters on the first day of early voting at the Lake County Government Center in Crown Point on Tuesday, Oct 6, 2026. (John Smierciak/for the Post-Tribune) 
 By Alexandra Kukulka | akukulka@chicagotribune.com | Post-Tribune PUBLISHED: November 13, 2026 at 4:22 PM CST Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... The Lake County Board of Elections and Registration reviewed provisional ballots for the 2026 midterm elections on Thursday, and the majority of the ballots that were rejected had signature and date issues.
 “Residents of Lake County can feel confident that the counting of votes is done correctly, efficiently and securely. All members of the board — whether Republican or Democrat — as well as the staff work tirelessly to ensure that’s the case,” said board president Kevin Smith.
 When reviewing the provisional absentee ballots, 32 ballots were rejected because voters did not return a signed affidavit confirming their identity. The board reviewed 42 provisional absentee ballots that did return an affidavit and rejected two ballots: one because the voter didn’t date the affidavit and one because of a signature discrepancy, said Lake County Board of Elections and Registration Director Michelle Fajman.
 The board rejected 54 provisional ballots filled out on Election Day that had having registration issues, like the voter no longer being registered at the address the office has on file.
 The board rejected five Election Day provisional ballots that required the voter to come to the office to show their identification card unless the voter came in with their ID by 12 p.m. Friday. Fajman said Friday afternoon that none of the voters came in with their IDs, so the ballots were rejected.
 When reviewing nine Election Day provisional ballots that were filed for name variations, the board initially accepted all of the ballots. But, after further review, four ballots were rejected because the ballots weren’t initialed by the poll worker, Fajman said.
 The board rejected eight Election Day provisional ballots that had date issues.
 The board accepted six absentee ballots that were received at early voting locations. The Griffith 10 precinct filed 14 emergency ballots, due to a power outage, and the board accepted those ballots.
 Eight emergency ballots cast at the Gary 5-04 precinct because of a power outage were rejected by the board because the ballots didn’t have proper poll worker initials.
 Michael Tolbert, the attorney for the Democratic members, said Indiana code would allow the board to accept the ballots as long as the members don’t believe the ballots were fraudulent.
 “We don’t want to disenfranchise the voter for poll worker error,” Tolbert said.
 Carly Brandenburg, the attorney for the Republican members, pointed to a court case ruling that stated poll workers initials are required to count provisional ballots.
 Board member Mara Candelaria Reardon voted against rejecting the Gary 5-04 ballots. She told the Post-Tribune she didn’t agree with rejecting the ballots because it disenfranchised voters “at no fault of their own.”
 Lake County Clerk Michael Brown said poll workers have to be trained to properly sign the emergency ballots.
 Board members work toward ensuring that ballots cast legally are counted, Smith said, and its members understand that sometimes voters do everything correctly but an error could occur somewhere else in the process, like poll worker error.
 Elections are run by people, which means a few instances of human error occur, Smith said. When reviewing the ballots that were rejected because of poll worker error, Smith said it did not appear to the board members that the mistakes were intentional and can be addressed in training.
 “We try to do everything we can to make sure that votes count,” Smith said.
